overview:
Mauna Ekadashi (also written Maun Ekadashi, Maun Agiyaras, Maunaikādaśī) is a Jain sacred observance that falls on the eleventh day (Ekadashi, Agiyaras) of the bright fortnight (Śukla pakṣa) of the lunar month Mārgaśīrṣa or Mārgashirsha. In many Gujarati-speaking communities it is known as Maun Agiyaras, literally “Silence Eleventh.” The core features of the day are voluntary silence (mauna), fasting (upavāsa or various graded fasts), intensified scriptural study, meditation, and remembrance of the Tirthankaras’ auspicious life-events (kalyāṇakas).

In Jain narrative and ritual literature, Mauna Ekadashi is singled out because multiple kalyāṇakas of several Tirthankaras are said to occur on this one tithi. A widely transmitted account states that five kalyāṇakas connected with three Jinas—Aranātha (often counted as the 18th in some lists, though more commonly the 17th), Mallinātha (19th), and Naminātha (21st)—fall on this day: Aranātha’s renunciation (dīkṣā), Mallinātha’s birth (janma), initiation (dīkṣā), and attainment of omniscience (kevalajñāna), and Naminātha’s kevalajñāna. Building on cosmological calculations across multiple regions (Bharata and Airāvata kṣetras) and time-cycles, later authors speak of a total of 150 kalyāṇakas occurring on this single Ekadashi, which is why the merit (puṇya) of austerities performed on this day is described as being multiplied many times over.

From the perspective of Jain ethics, Mauna Ekadashi is a practical exercise in restraining speech and desire. Jain doctrine treats speech as a powerful channel of karmic influx: gossip, harsh words, falsehood, and idle talk are all seen as forms of verbal himsā (harm) that disturb one’s own soul and others. By keeping mauna for a full day—often from sunrise to the following sunrise—practitioners aim to reduce the karmic load associated with careless speech, cultivate inner stillness, and redirect attention toward dharma. Silence is paired with fasting, which may range from complete abstention from food and water (cauvihāra upavāsa) to more moderate forms such as eating once (ekaśana) or twice (beyaśana) with simple, non-stimulating foods.

Ritually, Mauna Ekadashi is observed through a combination of vows and practices: maintaining silence except for necessary, carefully intentioned speech; undertaking a fast appropriate to one’s capacity and health; performing pratikramaṇa (ritual confession and reflection), listening to discourses, reading or reciting scriptures, and singing hymns in praise of the Jinas whose kalyāṇakas are commemorated. Importantly, traditional manuals clarify that scriptural recitation, devotional singing, and dharma discussion—when done mindfully—do not break the vow of mauna, because the vow is aimed at restraining frivolous and harmful speech rather than all sound.

In many lay communities, Mauna Ekadashi is taken as a niyama (regular vow) for a fixed number of years, often eleven, culminating in an udyāpana (formal completion ceremony). The day is sometimes described by later ācāryas as an “essence” of Jain festivals, because it concentrates in a single tithi the themes of renunciation, omniscience, and liberation that are spread across the calendar in other observances. While the observance is deeply valued, traditional texts and contemporary teachers alike emphasize that fasting and silence must be undertaken with due regard for health, age, and personal circumstances, and that questions of medical risk or major life decisions should be discussed with qualified human experts and lineage authorities.

Modern community literature and sermons often use Mauna Ekadashi to explore broader themes: the psychological effects of silence, the relationship between speech and nonviolence, and the relevance of mauna in contemporary life. Stories such as that of Suvrata Śreṣṭhī, and reflections on the silence of Mahāvīra, are used to illustrate how disciplined speech and inner listening can support the Jain path of self-restraint (saṃyama) and non-attachment (aparigraha). In this way, Mauna Ekadashi functions both as a specific calendrical festival and as a recurring reminder of the Jain ideal of mindful, non-harming communication.

primary_sources.title: Maunaikādaśīkathā (Mauna Ekadashi Kathā)
primary_sources.author: Anonymous Jain author; preserved in the Tessitori Collection
primary_sources.original_text: मौनैकादशी (मौन अग्यारस) मार्गशीर्ष शुक्ल पक्षस्य एकादश्यां भवति। तस्यां दिने त्रिजिनानां पञ्च कल्याणका भवन्ति—अरनाथस्य चक्रवर्तित्वत्यागदिक्षा, मल्लिनाथस्य जन्मदिक्षा-केवलज्ञानं, नमनाथस्य केवलज्ञानं।
primary_sources.transliteration: Maunaikādaśī (Mauna Agyāras) Mārgaśīrṣa śukla pakṣasya ekādaśyāṃ bhavati. Tasyāṃ dine trijinānāṃ pañca kalyāṇakā bhavanti—Aranāthasya cakravartitvatyāga-dīkṣā, Mallināthasya janma-dīkṣā-kevalajñānaṃ, Namanāthasya kevalajñānaṃ.
primary_sources.translation: “Mauna Ekadashi (Mauna Agyāras) falls on the eleventh day of the bright half of Mārgaśīrṣa. On that day five auspicious events of three Jinas take place: Aranātha’s initiation through renouncing his status as a Cakravartin; Mallinātha’s birth, initiation, and attainment of omniscience; and Naminātha’s attainment of omniscience.”
primary_sources.notes: This passage represents the kind of summary found in the Maunaikādaśīkathā, a Jain festival narrative text noted in manuscript catalogues such as the Tessitori Collection. It belongs to corpus tier A/B, as it reflects a traditional kathā genre grounded in Jain cosmology and hagiography. The wording above is a reconstructed Sanskrit-style formulation based on descriptions of the text; exact phrasing may vary between manuscripts and Prakrit/Sanskrit recensions. The key doctrinal content is the identification of Mauna Ekadashi with five kalyāṇakas of Aranātha, Mallinātha, and Naminātha, and its placement on Mārgaśīrṣa Śukla Ekādaśī.

primary_sources.title: Maun Ekadashi Vrat Katha
primary_sources.author: Compiled by Ācārya Vijay Jinendrasūri; published by Śrī Harṣ Puṣpamṛt Jain Granthmālā
primary_sources.original_text: भगवान् महावीरः गौतमस्वामिनं प्रति मार्गशीर्ष शुक्ल एकादश्यां पोषधधर्मस्य महिमानं कथयति—“यदि सर्वदा धर्मपालनं न शक्यते, तर्हि अस्यां तिथौ अल्पमपि धर्मकर्म महत्फलप्रदं भवति। नेमिनाथेनापि श्रीकृष्णराजाय उक्तं यत् एषा मौनैकादशी सर्वेषां व्रतानां सारभूता।”
primary_sources.transliteration: Bhagavān Mahāvīraḥ Gautamasvāminaṃ prati Mārgaśīrṣa śukla ekādaśyāṃ poṣadhadharmasya mahimānaṃ kathayati—“yadi sarvadā dharmapālanaṃ na śakyate, tarhi asyāṃ tithau alpam api dharmakarma mahatphalapradaṃ bhavati. Nemināthenāpi Śrīkṛṣṇarājāya uktaṃ yat eṣā Maunaikādaśī sarveṣāṃ vratānāṃ sārabhūtā.”
primary_sources.translation: “Lord Mahāvīra explained to Gautama Svāmi the greatness of the Poushad observance on the bright Ekadashi of Mārgaśīrṣa: ‘If one cannot uphold dharma continuously, then on this tithi even a small religious effort yields great fruit.’ Lord Neminātha likewise told King Kṛṣṇa that this Mauna Ekadashi is the essence of all vows.”
primary_sources.notes: The Maun Ekadashi Vrat Katha is a modern printed Jain text (tier B/D) that systematizes earlier narrative material and applies it to lay observance. It emphasizes the special merit of fasting and mauna on Mārgaśīrṣa Śukla Ekādaśī, recounts dialogues involving Mahāvīra, Gautama Svāmi, Neminātha, and Kṛṣṇa, and explains the calculation of 150 kalyāṇakas across multiple regions. The Sanskrit-style quotation above is a synthesized representation of themes reported in summaries of the text; the original is likely in Gujarati or mixed vernacular with scriptural citations. The text also details practical rules: chauvihār poṣadha (abstaining from all four types of consumables), permissible religious speech during mauna, and the equivalence of one day’s fast on Mauna Ekadashi to many ordinary fasts.

primary_sources.title: Community expositions on Maun Ekadashi (e.g., Kishor B. Shah, "Maun Ekadashi – Importance of Silence")
primary_sources.author: Kishor Bhimji Shah and other lay scholars
primary_sources.original_text: मौन एकादशी के दिन जो भी तप, उपवास, या शुभकर्म किया जाता है, उसका पुण्य डेढ़ सौ गुना माना जाता है। नेमिनाथ भगवान ने श्रीकृष्ण से कहा कि मौन एकादशी जैनों का सबसे महत्वपूर्ण पर्व है।
primary_sources.transliteration: Mauna Ekādaśī ke din jo bhī tapa, upavāsa, yā śubhakarma kiyā jātā hai, us kā puṇya ḍeṛh sau gunā mānā jātā hai. Neminātha Bhagvān ne Śrīkṛṣṇa se kahā ki Mauna Ekādaśī Jainon kā sabse mahatvapūrṇa parva hai.
primary_sources.translation: “On the day of Mauna Ekadashi, whatever austerity, fast, or virtuous deed is performed is believed to yield merit one hundred and fifty times greater. Lord Neminātha told Śrī Kṛṣṇa that Mauna Ekadashi is the most important festival of the Jains.”
primary_sources.notes: This represents the kind of didactic paraphrase found in community booklets and talks (tier D), such as Kishor B. Shah’s English and Gujarati materials circulated by Jain associations. These sources expand on traditional kathās, explain the 150-kalyāṇaka doctrine, and relate Mauna Ekadashi to other major festivals like Paryuṣaṇa and Dīpāvalī. While not primary canonical texts, they are influential in shaping contemporary lay understanding and practice. The quotation above is a reconstructed Hindi-style summary of points reported in such literature; exact wording varies by publication and language.

misconceptions.myth: Mauna Ekadashi requires absolute silence with no speech whatsoever, including recitation, prayer, or discussion of scriptures.
misconceptions.reality: Traditional Mauna Ekadashi manuals and vrat kathās distinguish between harmful, idle, or worldly speech and dharmic speech. The vow of mauna is aimed at restraining gossip, argument, boasting, and other forms of verbal himsā, not at prohibiting all sound. Scriptural study, devotional singing, and respectful dharma discussion—performed mindfully—are explicitly allowed and even encouraged on this day, because they support inner purification rather than karmic bondage.

misconceptions.myth: Every Jain is religiously obligated to perform a full waterless fast (chauvihār upavāsa) on Mauna Ekadashi, regardless of age, health, or circumstances.
misconceptions.reality: Jain texts present Mauna Ekadashi as a highly meritorious opportunity, not as an unconditional obligation for all. They describe a range of fasting options (complete fast, partial fast, limited meals) and emphasize that vows must be taken according to one’s capacity, health, and life situation. Contemporary teachers and community guides stress that those who are ill, pregnant, elderly, very young, or managing medical conditions should consult qualified medical professionals and religious mentors before undertaking severe austerities, and may observe the day through gentler practices such as moderated diet, reduced speech, and increased meditation.

misconceptions.myth: The statement that merit is multiplied 150 times on Mauna Ekadashi is a literal, mathematical guarantee of specific karmic outcomes.
misconceptions.reality: The “150 times” figure arises from cosmological and narrative calculations of kalyāṇakas across multiple regions and time-cycles, and functions primarily as a symbolic way of expressing the exceptional auspiciousness of the day. Jain doctrine treats karmic fruition as complex and dependent on many factors, including intention, purity of conduct, and prior karmic conditions. The multiplication metaphor should be understood as devotional and pedagogical, encouraging earnest practice, rather than as a precise numerical law of karma.

misconceptions.myth: Mauna Ekadashi is a minor, optional observance with no connection to core Jain teachings.
misconceptions.reality: While Mauna Ekadashi is not part of the eight-day Paryuṣaṇa cycle, traditional authors and later ācāryas describe it as an “essence” of Jain festivals because it concentrates key themes of renunciation, omniscience, and liberation in a single tithi. It commemorates multiple kalyāṇakas of Tirthankaras, foregrounds the ethical discipline of speech, and integrates fasting, meditation, and scriptural study. For many lay Jains, it is a central annual observance and is sometimes kept as a multi-year niyama culminating in a formal udyāpana ceremony.
